name: Don't over-pluck / regrow

lead: This is the grooming advice to stop tweezing so thin or gappy brow areas can fill in, giving fuller-looking brows over time. Tweezing is the most common way to shape brows.

Plucking pulls the hair from the follicle. Where follicles are not scarred, hair may regrow once the pulling stops; where they are scarred, loss can be permanent. No clinical studies specific to over-plucking were found.

paras: People put the tweezers down for a period, often several weeks to months, and fill gaps with pencil or powder in the meantime. Some limit shaping to trimming or clean-up of stray hairs only.

Persistent pulling can cause permanent hair loss, and over-tweezed brows are a recognized reason for transplant surgery. Brow loss can also signal an underlying condition, so persistent thinning is worth raising with a clinician.

angle.text: Stopping tweezing lets sparse brow areas fill in so brows look fuller over time. It works by letting dormant follicles resume growth, which depends on whether the follicles are still intact. No trials test it.

lead: "Don't over-pluck" is advice in looksmaxxing and grooming circles to stop tweezing eyebrows so that sparse areas can fill in. Tweezing is the most common way to shape brows, and Wikipedia notes that plucked hairs can stop growing back over time, though that statement is flagged as needing a citation.[1]

Hair loss from lashes and brows, called madarosis, depends on whether follicles survive: non-scarring loss may regrow when the cause is removed, while scarring loss is permanent and treated cosmetically, for example with transplantation.[2] Wikipedia also notes that people who have over-tweezed are considered candidates for eyebrow transplants, and that constant pulling of lashes can cause permanent damage.[1][3]
infobox: Eyebrow transplant, minoxidil (alopecia areata), prostaglandin analogs for lashes

paras: Tweezing, waxing and threading remove brow hairs, and men in Western societies have increasingly plucked parts of their brows.[1] Proponents of leaving brows alone say that frequent removal thins them over time and that leaving them untouched lets them recover.

Lashes pulled out take about seven to eight weeks to grow back, according to Wikipedia, and constant pulling may cause permanent damage.[3] Madarosis has many causes, including blepharitis, skin conditions, nutritional deficiency and hair-pulling disorders such as trichotillomania; its regrowth depends on whether follicles are scarred.[2] The madarosis article does not specifically discuss over-plucking.[2]
